1.2.2.4-f13.text: Non laudo eos qui in desipientia docent secandam esse venam frontis, quia spiritus debilitatur inde, & ego longa experientia observavi in proprio Xenodochio, quod desipientes ex Phlebotomia magis laeduntur, & magis desipiunt, & melancholici saepe fiunt inde pejores

translations.note: Xenodochium, literally a hostel for strangers, here means a hospital; Burton's main text calls Salvianus the 'Master of an Hospital of madmen'. Desipientia is folly or delirium; in this medical context it means madness.

burton_span.exact: and found by long experience, that this kind of evacuation, either in head, arm, or any other part, did more harm than good

source.author: Salustio Salviano (Salust. Salvianus)
source.basis: main text at the sidenote anchor: "Salust. Salvianus, lib. 2 cap. 1"

translations.text: I do not approve of those who teach that in madness the vein of the forehead should be opened, because the spirit is weakened by it; and I have observed by long experience in my own hospital that the mad are harmed more by bloodletting, and grow madder, and melancholic people are often made worse by it.

translations.note: Burton's main text names Salvianus (lib. 2 cap. 1) as master of a hospital of madmen, and this is that passage. Xenodochium means a hospice or hospital. Burton's English at the anchor gives only the gist (more harm than good), not the vein of the forehead or the weakening of the spirit.

translations.text: I do not approve of those who teach that, in madness, the vein of the forehead should be cut, because the spirit is thereby weakened; and I have observed by long experience in my own hospital that madmen are harmed more by bloodletting, and grow more mad, and melancholics often become worse from it.
